body: Welcome. Over about ninety days you will get one short note a day to help you steady yourself and hold on to your worth after losing a job.
Losing a job can feel like the floor has tilted. Whatever you feel right now, shock, relief, numbness or all three at once, it makes sense.
Notice how your body is carrying this news today. Tight shoulders, a heavy chest or restless legs: just name what you find without trying to fix it.
Redundancy is a decision about a role, a budget or a company structure. It was never a verdict on who you are as a person.
Shame often arrives uninvited after being let go. You do not have to argue with it; just recognise it as a feeling rather than a fact.
Grief is a reasonable response to losing work. You lost colleagues, routines and a place to belong, and missing them is completely normal.
Write one sentence that describes how you honestly feel this morning, in your own words. Nobody else ever needs to read it.
Anger can be a sign that something mattered to you. Let it be there, and give it a safe outlet, like a brisk walk or a furiously scribbled page.
Notice the story your mind keeps telling about what happened. Is it a fair account, or the harshest version it could find?
Plenty of capable, kind and talented people have been made redundant. You are in larger and better company than it may feel right now.
Get dressed this morning as if the day matters, because it does. Clean clothes quietly tell your mind that you are still showing up.
Some days you may feel steady and others flattened. Recovering from a loss rarely moves in a straight line, and that is alright.
Think about who you were before this job: the interests, jokes and quirks you carried. That person was never let go.
Look out for one moment when you feel a little lighter, even for a minute. Those small moments are worth collecting.
When people ask what happened, a short, simple answer is enough. You do not owe anyone the full story.
You might wake at your old start time and feel adrift. Let that hour become a gentle anchor rather than a reminder of what has gone.
Pick a regular time to get up for the rest of this week and keep to it kindly. Structure is a quiet form of self-care.
If this feels too heavy to carry alone, talking to someone you trust or to a professional is a sensible and courageous step.
Your worth was never stored in a job title, an email signature or a lanyard. It travels with you wherever you go.
Step outside for at least ten minutes before the afternoon. Daylight and fresh air will not solve everything, but they help more than you might expect.
Jot down three things you are good at that have nothing to do with your last job. Read the list back slowly.
Send a short message to one friend just to say hello. Connection matters more than ever right now, even in small doses.
Give your day a simple shape: something for the morning, something for the afternoon and rest in the evening.
Tidy one small corner of your home. A clear shelf or a sorted drawer is visible proof that you can still make things better.
Notice when you start measuring yourself against people who still have jobs. Gently bring your attention back to your own next small step.
Prepare one meal with a little more care than usual. Feeding yourself well is a simple act of self-respect.
If you keep replaying that last meeting, remind yourself softly that it happened, it is over, and you are still here.
Move your body in a way you enjoy for twenty minutes. Dance in the kitchen, stretch on the floor or walk around the block.
Some people around you may not know what to say. Their awkwardness is usually care that has not found its words yet.
List the people who would pick up if you rang them. Even one or two names make a real safety net.
It is alright to feel relief alongside the sadness. Mixed feelings do not make you ungrateful or confused, simply human.
Do one thing purely for pleasure, with no aim of being productive. Rest is not something you have to earn.
Days can feel shapeless without work. Choose one fixed point, a walk at ten or a cup of tea at three, and keep it.
Ask someone you trust what strengths they see in you. Listen to the answer without brushing it away.
Notice how often you describe yourself as just or only something. Try talking about yourself without those small shrinking words.
Check your phone and inbox at two set times rather than refreshing all day. Constant checking feeds worry more than it eases it.
Losing a job can loosen your sense of who you are. That loosening can also make room for parts of you that were squeezed out.
Revisit a hobby you set aside when work got busy. Ten minutes is enough to say hello to it again.
Sleep may be patchy for a while. Tonight, try a calm wind-down hour with dim lights and no screens before bed.
Offer a small kindness to someone else, a held door or a thoughtful message. Giving reminds you that you still have plenty to offer.
Write a short note to the version of you who first heard the news. What would you say to comfort them now?
Spend an hour somewhere people gather, like a library, park or café. Simply being around others can ease the sense of isolation.
When the thought that you have failed appears, try telling yourself that something has ended instead. One is a judgement; the other is simply true.
Notice one thing you handled well this week, however small. Give yourself honest credit for it.
You are allowed a slow day. Resting now does not mean you have given up on tomorrow.
Drink a glass of water, eat something nourishing and step into daylight. Tend to the basics before anything else.
If the heaviness is lingering or growing, reaching out to a doctor, counsellor or helpline is a wise and caring choice.
Learn one small new thing purely out of curiosity: a word, a recipe or a fact about the night sky.
Think of a time you got through something hard before. The same resourcefulness is still in you now.
Ring someone you like instead of texting. Hearing a familiar voice can steady you in a way that words on a screen cannot.
Notice what you miss most about working: people, purpose, rhythm or pride. Each of those can be fed in other ways too.
Name one value you care about, such as kindness, craft or honesty. Look for a small way to live it before bedtime.
Some days the hardest part is beginning. Pick the easiest possible first step and let that count as progress.
Sit somewhere comfortable for five minutes and breathe slowly, a little longer out than in. Let your shoulders drop as you go.
You are not behind. You are in a season of change, and seasons are not races.
Look for something small and regular to join, a walking group, a class or a volunteer shift. Belonging can be rebuilt one hour at a time.
Notice who drains you and who restores you at the moment. Lean a little more towards the people who leave you lighter.
Make a list of moments from your working life that you are proud of. Those achievements still belong to you.
Say no to one thing that would cost more energy than you have to spare. Protecting your strength is sensible, not selfish.
If you catch yourself apologising for being out of work, pause. There is nothing here to apologise for.
Plan something to look forward to this week, a film, a visit or a picnic. Hope grows faster when it has something to hold.
Your identity is far wider than your occupation. You are also a friend, a neighbour, a learner and someone who notices things.
Spend a few minutes outdoors noticing small details: birdsong, leaves, the shape of clouds. Attention to the world can quieten a busy mind.
Think back to your first week of these notes. Notice any small ways you feel steadier now, even if the change is subtle.
Imagine introducing yourself to a stranger without mentioning work. What would you choose to say first?
Make something with your hands, a sketch, a loaf or a repaired button. Making things is a reliable way to feel capable again.
Notice the routines you have built over these weeks. They are scaffolding you put up yourself, and they are holding.
Thank someone who has supported you since you were let go. A few honest words of gratitude strengthen you both.
Hard feelings may still visit, sometimes without warning. You now have ways to meet them, and they will pass again.
Listen to how you speak to yourself when something goes wrong. Try the tone you would use with a dear friend instead.
You are someone who went through a difficult loss and kept going. That is part of your story now, and a strong part.
Take a different route on your usual walk. A little novelty can remind you that change is not always a threat.
Write down three words that describe who you are becoming. Keep them somewhere you will see them often.
Share one honest feeling with someone you trust. Being known, even a little, is deeply steadying.
Your worth has not changed over these weeks, even though your circumstances did. It has been there all along.
Review your daily rhythm and keep whatever helps. Let go of one habit that no longer serves you.
Celebrate one small win out loud, even if the only audience is you. Small victories deserve to be noticed.
When old shame whispers, remind yourself how much courage you have shown through all of this. The evidence is on your side.
Spend time with someone who knew you long before this job. They remember the whole of you.
You have rebuilt routines, reached out to people and cared for yourself through hard days. That is real, quiet strength.
Watch for a moment today when you feel like yourself again. Let that feeling settle in for a while.
Whatever comes next, you will bring your character, your kindness and your experience with you. None of that was taken.
Write a short message to a future you who might face a setback someday. Tell them what you have learnt.
Notice how much more gently you hold this experience than you did at the start. Gentleness is a skill, and you have practised it.
Choose one routine you want to keep for good. Make it yours, whatever your circumstances become.
If heaviness still returns now and then, keep talking to people you trust. Seeking professional support remains an option whenever you need it.
Do something generous for your future self, like an early night or a tidy kitchen. You are worth looking after.
You are more than any role you have ever held. That was always true, and now you know it more deeply.
Consider the people, places and habits that helped you stand back up. Each one is part of your foundation now.
Look back over these ninety days. What have you learnt about yourself that you want to remember?
You have steadied yourself through something genuinely hard. Take a moment to recognise how far you have come.
This is the last note. Your worth was never held by a job, and the steadiness you rebuilt is yours to keep, so go gently.
